mcqs.q: The thyroid gland secretes:
mcqs.explain: The thyroid secretes T₄, T₃ and calcitonin; T₃/T₄ drive growth, metabolism and catecholamine effects.

mcqs.q: The single most useful marker of thyroid function is:
mcqs.explain: TSH (from the pituitary, via the hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis) is the most useful marker and is checked first.

mcqs.q: The commonest cause of hypothyroidism worldwide is:
mcqs.explain: Iodine deficiency is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism worldwide; Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the commonest autoimmune cause.

mcqs.q: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is:
opts: An autoimmune cause of hypothyroidism (B lymphocytes invade the thyroid)
mcqs.explain: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is autoimmune hypothyroidism in which B lymphocytes invade and destroy thyroid tissue.

mcqs.q: Which set of features fits HYPOthyroidism?
opts: Weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia and constipation
Weight loss, heat intolerance and tachycardia
mcqs.explain: Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance, bradycardia, constipation and depression, with a puffy face and dry skin.

mcqs.q: The biochemical pattern of primary hypothyroidism is:
mcqs.explain: In primary hypothyroidism, TSH is high (compensatory) while T₃/T₄ are low.

mcqs.q: Hypothyroidism is treated with:
opts: Levothyroxine (T₄), with caution in ischaemic heart disease
mcqs.explain: Levothyroxine (T₄) replaces the deficient hormone; caution is needed in IHD as it can exacerbate myocardial ischaemia.

mcqs.q: The most common cause of hyperthyroidism is:
mcqs.explain: Graves' disease accounts for ~76% of hyperthyroidism: IgG autoantibodies bind TSH receptors, driving gland hyperfunction.

mcqs.q: The mechanism of Graves' disease is:
opts: IgG autoantibodies binding TSH receptors to stimulate the gland
Destruction of the gland by B lymphocytes
mcqs.explain: In Graves' disease, IgG autoantibodies bind and stimulate TSH receptors, causing excess T₃/T₄ production.

mcqs.q: Which features fit HYPERthyroidism?
opts: Anxiety, tachycardia, weight loss and heat intolerance
mcqs.explain: Hyperthyroidism causes anxiety, tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, frequent stools and tremor, with low TSH and high T₃/T₄.

mcqs.q: The eye signs of Graves' disease include:
opts: A red painful eye with discharge
mcqs.explain: Graves' ophthalmopathy causes exophthalmos, lid retraction, a staring look and eye congestion.

mcqs.q: A goitre (enlarged thyroid) can be caused by:
opts: Iodine deficiency or excess, autoimmune thyroiditis, radiation or malignancy
mcqs.explain: Goitre arises from iodine deficiency/excess, autoimmune thyroiditis, lithium, radiation, infection or thyroid malignancy.

mcqs.q: Hyperthyroidism is treated medically with:
mcqs.explain: Symptomatic β-blockers plus carbimazole/propylthiouracil are used (50% relapse, risk of agranulocytosis); radio-iodine is an alternative.

mcqs.q: When investigating thyroid disease, a SUPPRESSED TSH indicates:
mcqs.explain: TSH is checked first: suppressed = hyperthyroid, elevated = hypothyroid; free T₄ confirms the picture.

mcqs.q: Why must epinephrine be used cautiously in a hyperthyroid dental patient?
opts: Elevated thyroid hormone makes them extremely sensitive to sympathomimetics (hypertensive crisis, dysrhythmia)
It has no effect in hyperthyroidism
mcqs.explain: High thyroid hormone increases sensitivity to sympathomimetics like epinephrine, risking hypertensive crisis, tachycardia and dysrhythmia.

mcqs.q: A dangerous emergency that dental stress can trigger in an uncontrolled hyperthyroid patient is:
mcqs.explain: Stress (e.g. dental surgery) can precipitate a thyroid storm in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, so elective care is deferred until controlled.

mcqs.q: Why is aspirin (ASA) contraindicated in hyperthyroidism?
opts: It displaces T₃/T₄ from protein binding, raising free hormone and worsening thyrotoxicosis
It lowers thyroid hormone too much
mcqs.explain: ASA interferes with the protein binding of T₃/T₄, increasing the free (active) hormone and worsening thyrotoxicosis.

mcqs.q: The anti-thyroid drug propylthiouracil (PTU) poses a bleeding risk because it has:
opts: A heparin-like action that is reversible
mcqs.explain: PTU has anti-vitamin-K activity causing hypoprothrombinaemia and a bleeding risk; patients must be evaluated before surgery.

mcqs.q: A rare but serious adverse effect of thionamides (carbimazole/PTU) affecting dental care is:
opts: Agranulocytosis, predisposing to oral infection and poor healing
mcqs.explain: Thionamides can cause agranulocytosis (~0.5%), leading to oral infections and inadequate wound healing.

mcqs.q: A classic ORAL finding of hypothyroidism is:
opts: Macroglossia with thickened lips and delayed wound healing
mcqs.explain: Hypothyroidism causes macroglossia, thickened lips, delayed eruption and delayed wound healing.

mcqs.q: Which drugs should be AVOIDED or used cautiously in a hypothyroid patient?
opts: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, narcotics) — risk of respiratory/cardiac depression
mcqs.explain: Benzodiazepines, barbiturates and narcotic analgesics can cause respiratory and cardiac depression in hypothyroid patients.

mcqs.q: Compared with euthyroid patients, hyperthyroid patients may be:
opts: Resistant to CNS depressants such as diazepam
Unable to receive any local anaesthesia
mcqs.explain: The increased sensitivity to catecholamines means hyperthyroid patients may be resistant to CNS depressants like diazepam.

mcqs.q: Congenital hypothyroidism in a child typically shows:
opts: Delayed tooth eruption, malocclusion and macroglossia
mcqs.explain: Congenital hypothyroidism causes developmental delay, delayed tooth eruption, malocclusion and macroglossia — needing early orthodontic referral.

mcqs.q: L-thyroxine (T₄) replacement therapy interacts with dental drugs by being:
mcqs.explain: L-thyroxine can be synergistic with sympathomimetic drugs used in dentistry, so vasoconstrictor use needs care.

saqs.q: Describe the thyroid hormones and the key screening test.
saqs.a: The thyroid secretes T₄, T₃ and calcitonin; T₃/T₄ drive growth, metabolism and catecholamine effects. TSH is the most useful screening test (high = hypo, suppressed = hyper).

saqs.q: List the causes and features of hypothyroidism.
saqs.a: Causes: iodine deficiency (commonest), Hashimoto's, iatrogenic, drugs (lithium/amiodarone). Features: weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia, dry skin, puffy face; high TSH, low T₃/T₄.

The commonest cause of hyperthyroidism (76%): IgG autoantibodies bind TSH receptors, driving gland hyperfunction. Features: anxiety, tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, exophthalmos/lid retraction; low TSH, high T₃/T₄.

saqs.q: Contrast the clinical features of hyper- and hypothyroidism.
saqs.a: Hyper: anxiety, tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, low TSH/high T₃-T₄. Hypo: depression, bradycardia, weight gain, cold intolerance, high TSH/low T₃-T₄.

saqs.q: Why is epinephrine and aspirin a concern in hyperthyroidism?
saqs.a: Epinephrine: elevated hormone causes extreme sensitivity to sympathomimetics → hypertensive crisis/dysrhythmia. Aspirin: displaces T₃/T₄ from protein binding, raising free hormone and worsening thyrotoxicosis.

saqs.q: List the dental considerations in hyperthyroidism.
saqs.a: Limit epinephrine; avoid aspirin; beware thyroid storm under stress; PTU has anti-vitamin-K (bleeding); thionamides → agranulocytosis/infection; patients may resist diazepam.

saqs.q: List the oral findings and dental cautions in hypothyroidism.
saqs.a: Macroglossia, thickened lips, delayed eruption/wound healing, malocclusion (congenital). Avoid CNS depressants (benzodiazepines/barbiturates/narcotics) — risk of respiratory/cardiac depression.
